title: Temperature Controls — Shift Leader Walk
description: This one teaches as much as it tests. You will calibrate your thermometer, temp real product on your make table, and work through what to do when something is out of temperature. Every standard here comes from the FSCC Guide. Take it standing in the kitchen with a thermometer and a cup of ice.

questions.title: Calibrate your thermometer now, then photograph it sitting in the ice bath.
questions.help:
Read this before you do it, because most people get it the wrong way round.

Fill a cup right to the top with ice. Then add water until it just fills the gaps. Stir it and let it sit about a minute.

What you are doing is getting THE WATER to 32°F. Ice packed tight with water around it sits at 32°F on its own — that is the whole trick.

Then you put the thermometer in and CHECK whether it reads 32°F. You are checking the thermometer against water you already know is 32°F.

You are NOT trying to make the thermometer say 32. That is the part people get wrong. Standing the stem in a cup of dry ice cubes with no water, waiting for the number to drop, and calling it calibrated does not work — there is no water holding a known temperature, so you have nothing to check it against.

FSCC 2.01: calibrate every thermometer each morning before food prep, and it has to be accurate to within 2°F.

questions.title: Which of these cups is the right ice bath for calibrating? Tap it.

hotspots.label: Packed full of ice, water filled in around it
hotspots.why: Ice packed to the rim with water around it is what holds the water at 32°F. That is the only one you can check a thermometer against.

questions.explanation: The cup packed full of ice with water added. The more ice, the longer the water holds steady at 32°F. The cups with only a little ice are mostly water sitting at room temperature — the reading will drift, and anything you check against it is wrong.

questions.title: A team member stands the thermometer stem in a cup of ice cubes with no water, waits for the number to stop moving, and says it is calibrated. What is wrong with that?
choices: Nothing — that is how you calibrate a thermometer
There is no water, so nothing is holding a known 32°F to check the thermometer against
They should have used hot water instead
They should have left it in for a full ten minutes
questions.explanation: Dry ice cubes have air gaps and no steady temperature. It is the ice AND water together that sit at 32°F. Without the water there is nothing to check the thermometer against, so the reading means nothing — and you are now temping product with a thermometer you only think is right.

questions.title: In a properly made ice bath your thermometer reads 36°F. What do you do?
choices: Nothing — 36°F is close enough
Adjust or replace it, and tell your manager
Use it anyway and take 4°F off every reading in your head
Put it back in the ice for longer until it reads 32°F
questions.explanation: FSCC 2.01 says a thermometer has to be accurate to within 2°F. 36°F is 4°F out, so it fails. Get it adjusted or swapped and tell your manager — every temperature taken with it until now was wrong by the same amount.

questions.title: Which kind of thermometer may NOT be used to take a product temperature?
choices: A digital thermocouple
A bi-metallic stem thermometer
A laser or infrared thermometer
A hanging thermometer
questions.explanation: FSCC 2.01: laser and infrared thermometers read the SURFACE only. They are fine for a quick check of a cooking surface, but they cannot tell you the internal temperature of food — and that is the one that matters.

questions.title: Now temp a cold product on your make table. What did it read, in °F?
questions.help: Pick any cold TCS product — diced ham, sausage, bacon, cheese. Put the probe into the middle of the product, not against the side of the pan. Dip the probe in sanitiser before you use it and between products.

questions.title: Photograph the thermometer in that product, with the reading visible.
What is the highest temperature cold TCS food is allowed to be held at?
questions.explanation: FSCC 2.03: cold TCS foods must be held at 41°F or below. Not 42. The make table's air temperature has to hold 41°F or less too (2.02).

questions.title: Four pans were just temped. Sauce 38°F. Pepperoni 40°F. Diced ham 47°F. Bacon 39°F. Which one is out of temperature?
choices: Sauce at 38°F
Pepperoni at 40°F
Diced ham at 47°F
Bacon at 39°F
questions.explanation: Diced ham at 47°F is 6°F over the limit. The other three are at or below 41°F and are fine. 40°F is not 'nearly out' — it is in standard.

questions.title: You have just found that diced ham at 47°F. What do you do? Pick everything that applies.
choices: Tell your manager straight away
Pull the product off the line now rather than at the end of the shift
Check whether the lid was left open or the pan was overfilled
Use the Cold Hold Temperature Verification Form to find the root cause
Top the pan up with fresh cold product to bring the temperature down
Stir it and temp it again in an hour
Nothing — ham is cured, so it is fine
questions.explanation:
Tell your manager — always, every time, before anything else. Then get it off the line and work out WHY, because the pan next to it is about to do the same thing. FSCC 2.03 points at the usual causes: lids left open, pans overfilled, too much product out of the cooler at once.

Topping the pan up with fresh product is the one that catches people. It does not cool anything down — it drags the fresh product up to the warm product's temperature, and now you have twice the problem.

questions.title: Your make table itself is not holding temperature — the air inside is reading 48°F. What do you do? Pick everything that applies.
choices: Tell your manager straight away
Record it on the Food Safety Checklist
Contact the service vendor for repair
Check the lids are closed and no wells are open without an insert pan or separator bar
Turn it to the coldest setting and carry on serving
Leave it until tomorrow and see if it sorts itself out
questions.explanation:
Tell your manager first — a make table that is not making temperature is their problem to act on, not something to work around quietly. Then record it, get the vendor called, and check the easy causes while you wait.

FSCC 2.02 is specific about open wells: every space needs an insert pan or a separator bar. An open well lets the cold fall straight out, and that alone can stop a table holding 41°F.

questions.title: Look at this make table. Tap what is wrong with it.

hotspots.label: An open well with no insert pan or separator bar
hotspots.why: FSCC 2.02: no open spaces on the make table without an insert pan or separator bar. The cold falls straight out of a gap like this.

questions.explanation: An open well with nothing in it. Cold air sinks, so a gap like this drains the whole rail and the pans either side start creeping up. Every space needs an insert pan or a separator bar, even when you are not using it.

questions.title: When do thermometers have to be calibrated?
choices: Every morning, before food prep starts
Once a week
Only when they look wrong
Whenever the FSCC Specialist asks to see it
questions.explanation: FSCC 2.01: every morning, before any food prep. The restaurant also has to have ice available to do it — bagged ice or filled ice trays count if there is no ice machine.

questions.title: In your own words: what are you actually trying to do when you calibrate a thermometer?
questions.help: No right answer to type here — your Area Coach reads these. If it is still fuzzy, go back to question 3 and read it again before you answer.
